div.p: he tied the horse to the knocker of the temple as if returning it, and on the next day stole it away. Now the man who did this died the most painful of deaths, by starvation; for though many fine dishes were set before him on the table, his bread and barley-cake seemed to have a foul stench, and he could not eat.

Many of us heard the hierophant tell this story. post λέγοντος sequuntur ὅτι Ἀνδοκίδης μηνύων τοὺς αὑτοῦ (αὐτοῦ Χ) συγγενεῖς καὶ φίλους ἀπώλλυε (ἀπολλύων Χk), φάσκων αὐτοὺς συνεργοὺς εἶναι· damnavit Reiske
It therefore seems right to me to recall now, in this man's case, what was said then, so that not only his friends may be ruined by him and his words, but he himself too by another.

It is impossible for you as well, when casting your vote on such a matter, either to pity or to favor Andocides, knowing as you do that these two goddesses manifestly punish τιμωρεῖτον Dobree: τιμωρεῖτε, τιμωρεῖται MSS.wrongdoers; every man must expect the same fate ταὐτὰ Thalheim: ὄντα MSS.for himself as for another.

Come, if Andocides now gets off scot-free from this trial through διʼ add. Scheibeyou, and enters the lot for the nine archons and draws the office of King Archon, will he not on your behalf both offer sacrifices θυσίας θύσει Cobet: θυσιάσουσι, θυσιάσει MSS.and utter prayers according to ancestral custom—some in the Eleusinium here, others in the sanctuary at Eleusis—and superintend the festival at the Mysteries to see that no one commits wrongdoing or impiety against the sacred rites?

And what opinion do you think the arriving initiates will hold when they see who the King Archon is and recall all his impieties—or the other Greeks who come ἔρχονται add. Reiskefor this festival wishing either to sacrifice at this gathering or to attend as spectators?

For Andocides is not unknown either abroad or at home because of his impieties; inevitably, men who perform deeds of extreme evil or good become well known. Moreover, he has plagued many cities in his travels—Sicily, Italy, the Peloponnese, Thessaly, the Hellespont, Ionia, Cyprus—and flattered many kings, whichever one he met, except Dionysius of Syracuse.

He is either the luckiest of all men or far surpasses the rest in judgment, since alone of those who dealt with Andocides he was not deceived by such a man, whose craft is to do no harm to his enemies, but all the harm he can to his friends. Consequently, by Zeus, it is not easy for you to grant him any unlawful favor without all Greece knowing.

Now, therefore, you must come to a decision about him; for you know well, men of Athens, that you cannot keep both your ancestral laws and Andocides—one of two things must be done: either erase the laws or get rid of the man.

He has reached such a pitch of audacity that he even claims about the law that the decree against him has been repealed and that he is now permitted to enter the Agora and the temples even now in the Council-chamber of the Athenians.

Yet they say Pericles once advised you regarding the impious to apply not only the written laws against them, but also the unwritten ones that the Eumolpidae expound, which no one has ever yet had the authority to repeal or dared to contradict, nor do men even know who enacted them; for thus, he thought, they would pay the penalty not only to men but to the gods as well.

Andocides, however, has shown such contempt for the gods and for those whose duty it is to avenge them that before he had been back in the city more or less μᾶλλον ἢ ἧττον del. Taylorten days, he brought an indictment for impiety before the King Archon—and got it registered, being ὢν add. ReiskeAndocides and having done what he has done against the gods—charging (so that you may pay closer attention) that Archippus Ἄρχιππον Palmer: Ἀρίστιππον MSS.had committed impiety against his own ancestral Herm! Archippus entered a counter-plea swearing that his Herm was sound and intact and had suffered none of what the other Herms suffered;

nevertheless, to avoid being harassed by such a character, he paid him money and got rid of him. Yet when this man saw fit to exact a penalty for impiety from another, surely it is just and pious for others to exact one from him!

He will say, however, that it is outrageous if the informer suffers the worst penalty while those he informed against enjoy full civic rights alongside you. Yet he will not be defending himself, but accusing the others as well. As for the others, those who ordered their restoration are in the wrong and guilty of the same impiety; but if you, being sovereign yourselves, ὅντες αὐτοί Reiske: ἦτε καὶ.are the ones who abolish the gods' vengeance, then you, not οὺχ add. Reiskethey, will be to blame. Do not choose, then, to turn this guilt upon yourselves when you can clear yourselves by punishing the wrongdoer.

Besides, they deny the charges informed against them, whereas this man admits he did it. Even in the Areopagus, the most august and just of courts, one who admits guilt is put to death, while if he disputes it he is put to the proof, and many have been found innocent. You must not, therefore, hold the same view of those who deny and those who confess. ὁμολογούντων Reiske: ὁμολογουμένων MSS.

It seems strange to me: if someone wounds a man's body—head, face, hands, or feet—he οὖτος Dobree: αὐτὸς MSS.shall be banished from the injured man's city under the laws of the Areopagus, post πόλιν in libris ἢ τραύματος ἐκ προνοίας· del. Taylorand if he returns, he shall be denounced and punished with death; yet if someone inflicts those very same injuries on the statues of the gods, will you not even bar him from setting foot in the temples, or fail οὐ add. Aldusto punish him when he enters? Surely it is both just and good to care for those from whom you can receive both good and evil.
They say that many of the Greeks also bar him from their own sanctuaries because of his impieties here; yet you yourselves, the ones wronged, value your own ordinances less than others value yours!

He has proved far more impious than Diagoras of Melos: the latter committed impiety in word against foreign rites and festivals, whereas this man did so in deed against those τὰ Aldus: τὰς MSS.of his own city. You ought therefore, men of Athens, to be angrier with citizens who wrong these sanctuaries than with foreigners; for the one is, as it were, an outsider's offense, the other a domestic one.

Do not acquit the wrongdoers you hold in your hands while trying to catch those in exile by proclaiming a reward of a talent of silver to anyone who brings them in or kills them; otherwise you will appear to the Greeks to be boasting rather than wanting to punish.

He also demonstrated to the Greeks that he does not believe in the gods: not as one afraid of what he had done, but with full confidence, he took up shipping and sailed the sea! Yet the god was leading him on, so that returning to the scene of his crimes he might pay the penalty at my instigation.

I hope he will indeed pay the penalty, nor would it surprise me at all, for the god does not punish immediately —rather that is human justice ἀλλ’ δίκηἀλλʼ del. Halbertsman—and I can infer this from many examples, seeing other impious men who paid the penalty in time, and their descendants too for their ancestors' sins. In the meantime the god sends many terrors and dangers upon wrongdoers, so that many have actually longed to die and be rid of their miseries; and at last, after ruining his life, the god imposes death.

Consider Andocides's own life since he committed impiety, and whether anyone else is like him. After Andocides sinned, brought before the court on a summary charge, ἐπιβολῆς Taylor: ἐπιβουλῆς MSS.he imprisoned ἔδησεν Stephanus: ἐδέησεν MSS.himself by proposing imprisonment as his penalty if he failed to produce his attendant—though he knew well he would not be able to produce him,

since the man had been put to death on his account and for his crimes so that he might not μὴ add. Stephanusbecome an informer! Surely some god deranged his mind, that he thought it easier to assess his penalty at imprisonment rather than money ἢ ἀργυρίου Taylor: μαρτυρίου MSS.with the same expectation!

As a result of this assessment he was kept in prison for nearly a year, and while imprisoned informed against his own kinsmen and friends, having been granted immunity if he were judged to have given true information. What state of mind do you think he was in when he was committing the most extreme and shameful acts by informing on his own friends, while his own safety remained uncertain?

After this, once he had brought death upon those he himself claimed to value most, he was judged to have given true information and was released, and you further decreed that he be barred from the Agora and the temples, so that even when wronged by his enemies he could not obtain legal redress.

Never yet, πω Reiske: που MSS.as long as Athens Ἀθῆναι Bekker: Ἀθηναίων MSS.has been remembered, has anyone been disfranchised on such a charge—and rightly so, for no one ever yet committed such deeds. And should we attribute these things to the gods or to chance?
After this he sailed to the king of Citium, was caught betraying him, and was imprisoned; he feared not only death, but daily tortures as well, expecting to have his extremities cut off alive.

Escaping from that danger, he sailed back to his own city under ἐπὶ Taylor: ἐπεὶ MSS.the Four Hundred— for such γὰρ add. Taylor, τοσαύτην ετ ὁ Marklandoblivion did the god send upon him that he actually longed to come back among the very people he had wronged! Upon arriving he was imprisoned and tortured, yet did not perish, and was released.

From there he sailed to Evagoras, king of Cyprus, committed a crime, and was locked up. Escaping from him too, ἀποδρὰς δὲ καὶ Reiske: ἀποδράσας MSS.he fled the gods here, he fled his own city, and he fled the very places he first reached! What joy is there in life, to suffer hardships constantly and never find rest?

Sailing back from there to this democracy to his own city, εἰς πόλιν del. Dobreehe bribed the prytaneis to introduce him here, and you drove him out of the city, upholding for the gods the laws you had decreed.

No democracy, no oligarchy, no tyrant, no city is willing to receive the man permanently; instead, ever since his impiety, he spends his whole time wandering, always trusting strangers more than acquaintances because he has wronged everyone he knows. And now, having finally come back to the city, he has been denounced twice in the same year.

His body is constantly in chains, and his property dwindles from his trials. Yet καίτοι Markland: καὶ MSS.when a man parcels out his substance to his enemies and informers, that is living ζῆν Cobet: τὸν MSS.a life not worth living—schemes which the god puts into his head not for his salvation, but in punishment for his past impieties.

And finally now he has surrendered himself to you to treat as you wish, not trusting in his innocence, but driven by some divine compulsion. Surely, by Zeus, neither older nor younger men, seeing Andocides surviving his perils while knowing he has committed unholy deeds, ought to become less pious—reflecting that half a life lived without misery is better than twice as long lived in misery, like this man.

He has reached such shamelessness that he is even preparing to engage in politics, τὰ πολιτικὰ πράττειν Valckenaer: τῆ πόλει καὶ πράττει MSS.and already addresses the Assembly, criticizes and challenges the scrutiny of certain magistrates, and enters the Council to give advice on sacrifices, revenues, prayers, and oracles! Yet if you follow his advice, which gods will you think you are pleasing? Do not suppose, gentlemen of the jury, that if you choose to forget what he has done, the gods will forget too!

He does not see fit to live quietly in the city as a guilty man, but carries on as if he himself had uncovered those who wronged the city, scheming to gain greater influence than others ἑτέρων Contius: ἑτέρους, ἑτέρως MSS.—as though it were not solely through your mildness and preoccupation that he has not yet paid the penalty to you, against whom he now offends in plain sight, only to be exposed and punished at the same time.

He will also rely heavily on this argument—for it is necessary ἔχει Franz: ἔχω MSS.to inform you what his defense will be, so that having heard both sides you may judge better: he claims he did the city a great service by informing and freeing it from the fear and turmoil of that time. But who caused those great evils?

Was it not this very man, by doing what he did? Must we then thank him for the good because he informed—when you paid him immunity as his wage—while you are to blame for the turmoil δὲ ταραχῆς Schott: δ’ ἀρχῆς.and the evils because you sought out the impious? Certainly not—quite the opposite: he threw the city into turmoil, and you restored order.

I hear he intends to argue in his defense that the amnesty agreements apply to him too, just as to the rest of the Athenians; using this as a pretext, he thinks many of you, afraid of breaking the agreements, will acquit him.

I will therefore explain how Andocides has no share in the agreements—neither, by Zeus, in those you made with the Lacedaemonians, nor in those ὧν Reiske: τῶν MSS.made by the men from Piraeus with those in the τῷ del. Pertzthe city. For none of us, numerous as we were, had offenses the same as or similar to those of Andocides, such that he too should benefit from us.

Nor indeed were we quarreling on his account and then reconciled once we gave him a share in the agreements! It was not for one man's sake, but for our own sake—those from the city and from Piraeus—that the agreements and oaths were made; it would be absurd if, when we ourselves were in distress, we had taken care of Andocides while he was abroad so as to wipe out his crimes!

Perhaps the Lacedaemonians looked out for Andocides in their treaty because they received some benefit from him—or did you look out for him? In return for what service? Because he often risked his life for you on behalf of the city?

This defense of his is not true, men of Athens—do not be deceived. It is not breaking the compact if Andocides pays the penalty for his private crimes, but only if someone punishes another privately on account of our public disasters.

Perhaps he will also bring counter-charges against Cephisius, and he will have plenty to say—for one must speak the truth. Yet you cannot punish both the defendant and the prosecutor with the same vote! Now is the time to judge this man justly; another time will come for Cephisius and for each of us whom he mentions today. Do not, therefore, out of anger at someone else, acquit this guilty man now.

He will also say that he turned informer and no one else will be willing to inform for you if you punish him. Yet Andocides has already received his informer's reward from you, having saved his own life while others died because of it! You are responsible for his survival, while he himself is responsible for these present troubles and perils, having violated the decrees and the terms of immunity under which he turned informer.

You must not grant informers license to break the law (what they have done is enough), but punish them when they transgress. Other informers, all who were caught on shameful charges and informed on themselves, know at least one thing: not to bother those they wronged, thinking that abroad they will pass as Athenians in full standing, whereas at home among the citizens they wronged they will be seen as wicked and impious.

Why, Batrachus—the most wicked man of all except this one—who turned informer under the Thirty and had agreements and oaths just like the men of Eleusis, nonetheless feared those of you he had wronged and lived in another city. Andocides, who wronged the gods themselves, showed less respect for them by entering their temples than Batrachus showed for men! Surely someone more wicked and more brazen than Batrachus ought to be only too glad to be spared by you!

Come now, in view of what εἰς τί Markland: εἴ τι.should you acquit Andocides? As a good soldier? He has never once campaigned from the city—neither as cavalryman nor hoplite, neither as trierarch nor marine, neither before the disaster nor after the disaster—though he is over forty years old!

Yet καίτοι Auger: καὶ MSS.other exiles in the Hellespont served as joint trierarchs for you. Recall yourselves out of how many evils and wars you rescued yourselves and the city, toiling hard with your bodies, spending much money both privately and publicly, and burying many brave citizens because of the war.

Andocides, having suffered none of these evils Post γενόμενος add οὐδὲν συμβαλόμενος Cobetfor the salvation of his country, now claims a share in the city while committing impiety in it. Because he is rich, powerful with money, and a guest-friend of kings and tyrants—things he will boast of now, knowing your ways—what property tax could be of benefit to him,

when, knowing the city was in great storm and peril, though he was a shipowner he did not have the heart to help his country by importing grain? Instead, metics and foreigners helped the city by importing it εἰσαγαγὼν, εἰσαγαγόντες MSS.out of regard for their resident status; while you, Andocides—what good have you done, what sins have you redeemed, what return for your nurture have you paid back

Athenians, remember what Andocides has done, and think also of the festival for which you have been honored above most men. Yet you have become numb to his sins from seeing and hearing of them so often, so that even terrible things no longer seem terrible to you. Pay attention, let your minds picture what he used to do, ἐποίει Taylor: ποιεῖ MSS.

and you will judge better. Putting on a ceremonial robe, he mocked the sacred rites, displayed them to the uninitiated, and spoke aloud the forbidden words; and the gods whom we recognize as gods θεοὺς del. Dobreeand worship with purification, sacrifice, and prayer—these he mutilated! For this, priestesses and priests stood facing the west, cursed him, and shook out their crimson robes according to ancient and ancestral custom.

He confessed to doing it. Furthermore, transgressing the law you enacted—that he be barred from the sanctuaries as an accursed sinner—forcing his way past all this, he has entered our city, sacrificed at altars forbidden to him, attended the sacred rites against which he committed impiety, entered the Eleusinium, and washed his hands from the sacred basin! Who ought to tolerate this?

What friend, what kinsman, what fellow demesman δημότην Blass: δικαστὴν MSS.should secretly favor this man and openly incur the hatred of the gods? Now, therefore, you must consider that in punishing and ridding yourselves of Andocides you are purifying Post καθαίρειν in libris ἀρὰν ἀπάγεσθαι del. Taylorthe city, averting pollution, casting out a scapegoat, and ridding yourselves of an accursed wretch—for he is one of these.

I wish to tell you, then, what Diocles, son of Zacorus the hierophant and our grandfather, advised you when you were deliberating how to deal with a Megarian who had committed impiety. When others urged putting him to death on the spot without trial, he advised trying him—for men's sake, so that hearing and seeing, others might behave more discreetly, and for the gods' sake, so that each juror might come into court having already decided in his own heart at home what the impious man deserves to suffer.

You too, men of Athens (for you know what must be done), do not be talked over by him; you have caught him clearly in impiety—you have seen and heard his crimes. He will beg and implore you; show no pity, for it is not those who die justly, but those who die unjustly, who deserve pity.
